title: Drive belts and stern gear
summary: The belts that drive the alternator and pumps, the gearbox, and everything between the gearbox and the water: shaft, coupling, stern gland and propeller.

lessons.title: Drive belts
lessons.intro: A rubber belt on the front of the engine drives the alternator and, on many engines, the coolant circulating pump. A belt that fails can stop the charging and overheat the engine at the same time, so it deserves regular attention.
lessons.caution: Never touch or check a belt while the engine is running. Belts and pulleys can trap fingers, hair and clothing in an instant. Make sure the engine cannot be started before you inspect them.

steps.title: What the belts drive
steps.text: Find out what each belt on your engine turns. Usually it is the alternator and the coolant pump; on some engines the raw water pump too. That tells you what will stop working if the belt breaks.

steps.title: Types of belt
steps.text: Older and smaller engines often use a V-belt, which grips by its sloping sides. Many newer engines use a flat ribbed belt, sometimes called poly-V or multi-rib. They are not interchangeable.

steps.title: Inspecting a belt
steps.text: With the engine stopped and unable to start, look along the whole belt. Cracks across the ribs, fraying edges, a shiny glazed surface or black rubber dust around the pulleys all suggest it needs replacing.

steps.title: Tension
steps.text: A slack belt slips and squeals and wears quickly. A belt that is too tight overloads the bearings in the alternator and pump. Your handbook explains how to check tension on your engine, usually by how far the belt moves when pressed at a given point.

steps.title: Adjusting and replacing
steps.text: On many engines the tension is set by moving the alternator on its mounting and locking it in place; others have an automatic tensioner. Follow your engine maker's instructions for the type of belt, its tension and when to check it again after fitting: new belts often need re-tensioning after a short period of running as they bed in.

steps.title: Carry a spare
steps.text: Keep a spare belt of the right type and size on board, along with the tools to fit it. Check it fits before you need it.

lessons.reviewNote: Audit note 22, accept with qualification: tensioning, re-tensioning and belt type now explicitly follow the engine maker. Please approve.

lessons.title: The gearbox
lessons.intro: The gearbox lets the engine run while the propeller is stopped, and lets you choose ahead or astern. It also reduces the speed of the shaft so the propeller turns at an efficient speed.

steps.title: What it does
steps.text: The gearbox has three positions: ahead, neutral and astern. In neutral the engine can run without turning the propeller. Most marine gearboxes also reduce the shaft speed compared with the engine speed.

steps.title: Gearbox oil
steps.text: Most gearboxes have their own oil, separate from the engine oil, with their own dipstick or level plug. Some use engine oil and some use other types such as transmission fluid. Use only what the handbook specifies, and check the level as often as it advises.

steps.title: Changing gear
steps.text: Change gear only with the engine at idle and, where your gearbox handbook supports it, pause briefly in neutral when going between ahead and astern so the shaft can slow down. Slamming between ahead and astern at high revs strains the gearbox and couplings.

steps.title: The gear cable
steps.text: A cable usually connects the gear lever to the gearbox. If it stretches or its fixings work loose, the gearbox may not fully engage or fully return to neutral. Check the lever positions match the gearbox lever at each end of its travel. A slight drag in neutral when cold can be normal on some gearboxes, but the boat should not drive steadily ahead or astern in neutral.

steps.title: Signs of trouble
steps.text: Slipping or delayed engagement, new noises, a burning smell or oil leaking around the gearbox are all reasons to stop and investigate, and probably to get specialist advice.

lessons.reviewNote: Audit note 23, accept with qualification: the neutral pause applies where the gearbox handbook supports it. Step 4 now distinguishes normal slight cold drag from positive drive (note 24). Please approve.

lessons.title: The stern gland
lessons.intro: Where the propeller shaft passes out through the hull, a seal called the stern gland keeps the water out. There are two main kinds, and each needs a different sort of care.
lessons.caution: Never adjust or touch the stern gland while the shaft is turning. Make sure the engine is stopped and cannot be started.

steps.title: The traditional packed gland
steps.text: A traditional gland, often called a stuffing box, squeezes rings of packing around the shaft. The packing is lubricated and cooled by water, so many are designed to drip slightly while the shaft turns; how much is acceptable depends on the gland and its maker. Some have a greaser that you turn to push grease into the packing.

steps.title: Mechanical shaft seals
steps.text: Many modern boats use a mechanical shaft seal, with a face or lips running on the shaft, designed not to drip. They are usually held by a short length of flexible hose. Some need venting after launch or at intervals, as described by the seal's maker.

steps.title: Daily check
steps.text: Look at the stern gland as part of your checks, and again after a long passage. Know what is normal for your seal type: a slow drip from a packed gland may be normal, while a steady leak from a seal designed not to drip is not. Treat any new or increasing leak as urgent: check the bilge and make sure your bilge pumping can keep up.

steps.title: Adjusting a packed gland
steps.text: Only with the engine stopped and the shaft unable to turn, a packed gland that leaks too much can be adjusted by tightening its nuts a little and evenly, as its maker describes. Too tight and it will overheat and wear the shaft. Follow the maker's advice for how much drip to aim for, and when to repack it. Never adjust it around a rotating shaft.

steps.title: Hoses and clips
steps.text: Check the flexible hose that holds the gland or seal for cracks and perishing, and check its clips. This hose is below the waterline.

lessons.reviewNote: Audit note 25, revise (S11): drip rates, venting and adjustment are now product-specific; new or increasing leakage is treated as urgent with a bilge pumping check; adjustment only with the shaft unable to turn. Please approve.

lessons.title: Shaft, coupling and propeller
lessons.intro: The propeller shaft carries the engine's power out through the hull to the propeller. Most problems here show up as vibration, noise or a change in how the boat handles.
lessons.caution: Before anyone goes near the propeller, in the water or out of it, stop the engine and make sure it cannot be started.

steps.title: The coupling
steps.text: The shaft is bolted to the gearbox through a coupling. Some installations use a flexible coupling to absorb small movements and reduce noise. The bolts must stay tight.

steps.title: Alignment and engine mounts
steps.text: The engine sits on flexible mounts, and it has to be lined up accurately with the shaft. Worn or collapsed mounts, or poor alignment, cause vibration and wear the cutless bearing and stern gland.

steps.title: The cutless bearing
steps.text: Where the shaft leaves the hull, it runs in a rubber-lined bearing lubricated by the water outside. When the boat is out of the water, noticeable sideways movement of the shaft in this bearing is one clue that it is worn; check it against the bearing maker's tolerances or ask an engineer.

steps.title: The propeller
steps.text: Barnacles, weed or a damaged blade reduce performance and can cause vibration and black smoke as the engine labours. Inspect and clean the propeller whenever the boat is lifted out. Many boats also have a sacrificial anode on the shaft that needs replacing when worn.

steps.title: Rope round the propeller
steps.text: A rope or net caught round the propeller can stall the engine or cause heavy vibration. Some boats carry a rope cutter on the shaft. Never try to clear the propeller unless the engine is stopped and cannot be started.

steps.title: Noticing change
steps.text: Get to know how your boat normally feels and sounds under power. New vibration, knocking or a drop in speed for the same engine revs are all worth investigating.

lessons.reviewNote: Audit note 27, accept with qualification: shaft play is now described as one clue, to be checked against the bearing maker's tolerances. Please approve.

questions.prompt: On many engines, what two things stop working if the alternator belt breaks?
options: Battery charging and the coolant circulating pump
The fuel lift pump and the fuel injection pump
The engine oil pump and the starter motor
The gearbox and the stern gland greaser
questions.explanation: A single belt often drives both the alternator and the coolant pump, so a broken belt can mean no charging and rapid overheating together.

questions.prompt: What is the safe way to inspect a drive belt?
options: With the engine stopped and unable to be started
With the engine at idle so you can see it moving
With the engine at high revs to check for slipping
While someone else holds the start button
questions.explanation: Belts and pulleys can trap fingers and clothing instantly. Inspect only with the engine stopped and the key removed or isolator off.

questions.prompt: You find fine black rubber dust around the pulleys. What does it usually mean?
options: The belt is wearing, possibly from slipping or misalignment
The engine oil is old and needs changing soon
Soot is leaking from the exhaust elbow into the engine space
The fuel filter is shedding its paper element
questions.explanation: Rubber dust comes from the belt itself wearing away. Check the tension, the pulley alignment and the belt's condition.

questions.prompt: Why is a belt that is too tight a problem?
options: It overloads the bearings in the alternator and pump
It makes the belt slip and squeal under load
It stops the starter motor from turning the engine over
It makes the engine burn noticeably less fuel
questions.explanation: Over-tightening puts a constant sideways load on the bearings of whatever the belt drives, wearing them early. Slipping and squealing come from a belt that is too slack.

questions.prompt: Why should the tension of a newly fitted belt be checked again after a short period of running?
options: New belts bed in and stretch slightly, so they can become slack
New belts shrink as they warm up and become too tight
The alternator creeps further away from the engine as it wears
The first run can flip the belt over so it sits the wrong way round
questions.explanation: A new belt settles into its pulleys and stretches a little at first. Rechecking catches the extra slack before it starts to slip.

questions.prompt: What lets the engine run while the propeller is not turning?
options: Putting the gearbox in neutral
Closing the raw water seacock fully
Loosening the stern gland
Switching off the alternator
questions.explanation: In neutral the gearbox disconnects the engine from the shaft, so the engine can warm up or charge the batteries without driving the boat.

questions.prompt: What is the right way to change from ahead to astern?
options: Bring the engine to idle, pause briefly in neutral, then select astern
Go straight from ahead to astern without changing the revs
Stop the engine, select astern, then restart the engine
Raise the revs in neutral, then select astern quickly
questions.explanation: Changing at idle with a short pause lets the shaft slow before the gearbox engages the other direction, avoiding shock loads on the gearbox and coupling. Follow your gearbox handbook if it says otherwise.

questions.prompt: Where should you check the gearbox oil level on most installations?
options: On the gearbox's own dipstick or level plug
On the engine oil dipstick, because they share oil
In the coolant header tank
In the fuel filter bowl
questions.explanation: Most gearboxes have their own separate oil supply with its own dipstick or level plug, and may need a different type of oil from the engine.

questions.prompt: With the engine warm and the lever in neutral, the boat drives steadily forward as if in gear. What is a likely cause?
options: The gear cable is out of adjustment
The engine's idle speed is set slightly too high
The cutless bearing is worn and lets the shaft drag
The propeller is fouled with weed
questions.explanation: If the cable has stretched or slipped, the lever and gearbox positions no longer match, and the gearbox may stay partly engaged. Some gearboxes drag slightly in neutral when cold, which can be normal, but steady drive in neutral is not. Idle speed, bearing wear and fouling do not make a gearbox drive in neutral.
questions.reviewNote: Audit note 24, revise: the question now describes steady drive with a warm engine, and the explanation separates normal slight cold drag from positive drive. Please approve.

questions.prompt: Apart from ahead, neutral and astern, what else does a marine gearbox usually do?
options: Reduces the shaft speed compared with the engine speed
Charges the batteries through a second alternator
Cools the engine oil before it returns to the engine sump
Pumps raw cooling water through to the engine
questions.explanation: Propellers work best turning slower than a diesel engine, so most gearboxes include a reduction ratio.

questions.prompt: What is the job of the stern gland?
options: To keep water out where the shaft passes through the hull
To connect the shaft to the gearbox output flange
To cool the gearbox oil using the water outside
To hold the propeller firmly on the tapered end of the shaft
questions.explanation: The shaft has to pass through the hull to reach the propeller. The stern gland seals around it while still letting it turn.

questions.prompt: A traditional packed stern gland drips slowly while the shaft turns. What does this usually mean?
options: It may be normal: many packed glands use water to cool and lubricate
The gland should be tightened straight away until all dripping stops
The packing has failed and the gland needs repacking now
The cutless bearing has worn and needs replacing
questions.explanation: Many packed glands are meant to drip slightly in use; how much is normal depends on the gland and its maker. Tightening until all dripping stops can overheat the packing and wear the shaft. A new or increasing leak is different: treat it as urgent.
questions.reviewNote: Audit note 26, accept with qualification (S11): a small drip while turning may be normal for some packed glands; the explanation makes drip rates product-specific. Please approve.

questions.prompt: What can happen if a packed stern gland is tightened too much?
options: The packing overheats and wears a groove in the shaft
The propeller works loose and eventually falls off the shaft
The gearbox can no longer be put into gear
The gland stops dripping and the shaft runs cooler
questions.explanation: Too much pressure stops the water reaching the packing. Friction then heats it and wears the shaft, which can be costly to repair. A dry gland is not a sign that all is well.

questions.prompt: A shaft seal that its maker says should not drip shows a steady trickle of water. How should you treat it?
options: As an urgent fault, checking the bilge pumps can keep up
As normal, because every kind of shaft seal drips a little
As a sign that the seal needs more grease pumping in
As something to look at when the boat is next lifted out
questions.explanation: A seal designed not to drip should stay dry. A leak can mean wear, damage or a problem with its hose, and it is below the waterline, so new or increasing leakage is a vessel-safety issue: check the bilge, make sure the pumps can keep up and get the seal looked at.
questions.reviewNote: S11: the key now treats leakage from a seal designed not to drip as urgent and adds the bilge pumping check. Please approve.

questions.prompt: When is it safe to adjust the stern gland?
options: Only with the engine stopped and unable to be started
Only while the shaft is turning slowly in gear
Only with the engine running in astern at idle
At any time, because the shaft is safely behind a guard
questions.explanation: A turning shaft can catch clothing, fingers or tools. Make sure it cannot turn before working near it.

questions.prompt: After a passage the bilge is filling faster than usual, and water is coming from the shaft seal. What should you do first?
options: Stop the shaft once safe, check the pumps keep up, and get help if it gains
Tighten the seal with the shaft turning so you can see the leak slow down
Keep motoring to harbour and look at the seal when next lifted out
Pump the bilge dry and carry on unless the leak gets worse
questions.explanation: An uncontrolled leak at the shaft seal is a vessel-safety issue. Stop the shaft once it is safe, make sure pumping keeps up, and call for assistance early if the water is gaining. Never adjust a seal on a turning shaft.
questions.reviewNote: New in content 1.1 (S11, S20): a safety-first scenario on shaft-seal leakage, matching the Fault finder stop card. Please approve.

questions.prompt: A rope has wrapped round the propeller. What must you do before trying to clear it?
options: Stop the engine and make sure it cannot be started
Put the engine in astern to unwind it
Run the engine at full power ahead to cut through it
Leave the engine in neutral while you clear it
questions.explanation: Even in neutral, a gearbox can drag or be knocked into gear. Stopping and isolating the engine is the only safe state for working near the propeller.

questions.prompt: What lubricates a typical cutless bearing?
options: The water the boat is floating in
Engine oil pumped from the sump
Grease from the stern gland greaser
Gearbox oil
questions.explanation: The cutless bearing has a grooved rubber lining that lets water flow through, lubricating and cooling it.

questions.prompt: With the boat out of the water, the shaft can be moved sideways in the bearing where it leaves the hull. What does this suggest?
options: The cutless bearing may be worn
The stern gland packing needs adjusting
The shaft anode has worn away
The gearbox oil is low
questions.explanation: A good bearing supports the shaft closely, so noticeable sideways movement is a clue that the rubber lining has worn. Check it against the bearing maker's tolerances, or ask an engineer.

questions.prompt: Why can a fouled propeller make the engine produce black smoke?
options: The extra load calls for more fuel than the air can burn cleanly
Barnacles on the propeller release oil that is drawn into the exhaust
The fouling blocks the exhaust outlet under the water
Weed is drawn into the engine's air filter and clogs it
questions.explanation: Extra drag means more load. The engine is supplied with more fuel to keep its speed, but there is not enough air to burn it all, which shows as black smoke.

questions.prompt: Over a season, vibration under power slowly gets worse and the stern gland starts to leak more. What should you suspect?
options: Worn engine mounts or poor alignment between engine and shaft
Too much oil left in the engine after the last oil change
A fuel filter that is slowly blocking with sludge
A weak engine battery that is losing its charge
questions.explanation: If the engine sags on worn mounts or is out of line with the shaft, the shaft runs off-centre, causing vibration and wearing the gland and cutless bearing.
